title: Open Quantum Systems Toolkit
intro: A quantum reservoir is an open quantum system driven by data: each input step is a quantum channel, its memory is the way that channel forgets, and its output is a noisy estimate of expectation values. This topic collects the open-system machinery the rest of the shelf uses, past the closed-system, pure-state picture of a first quantum computing course.

blocks.text: Why a reservoir has to be open

A closed system evolves unitarily, and unitary maps preserve the distance between states: $D(U\rho U^\dagger, U\sigma U^\dagger) = D(\rho,\sigma)$. A reservoir built from unitaries alone therefore never forgets its initial state, and two runs that started differently stay exactly as distinguishable as they were, forever. Reservoir computing needs the opposite: the state after a long input history must depend on the recent inputs and not on where it started (the echo state property, see The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property)). Forgetting requires discarding information, and in quantum mechanics that means coupling to something you then trace out: an environment, a reset qubit, a measurement whose result is ignored. So every working quantum reservoir is an open system, whether the openness is engineered (resetting an input qubit), natural (T1 and T2 decay on hardware) or comes from measurement.

The state is a density operator $\rho \ge 0$, $\operatorname{Tr}\rho = 1$, on $\mathcal{H} = (\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}$, $d = 2^n$. One input step $s_k$ acts as a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map, a channel:

blocks.caption: An input-driven quantum reservoir is a sequence of channels chosen by the data (Kraus form).

blocks.text: In continuous time the channel is generated by a Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) master equation:

blocks.caption: Lindblad form: Hamiltonian part plus dissipators with jump operators $L_j$.

blocks.text: Memory is controlled by how strongly these channels contract the trace distance $D(\rho,\sigma) = \tfrac12\Vert\rho-\sigma\Vert_1$. If every input channel contracts by at least a factor $\eta<1$, the dependence on the initial state dies as $\eta^k$:

blocks.caption: Uniform contraction gives the echo state property and fading memory.

blocks.text: The readout is a linear function of expectation values $x_i = \operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$, which hardware can only estimate from a finite number $S$ of shots, each one a measurement that disturbs the state. The statistical error is of order $1/\sqrt{S}$; the disturbance is what makes time series hard on real devices (see Measurement Back-Action (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action)).

items: Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels): mixed states, partial trace, the Pauli (Bloch) representation and why it is the reservoir's feature space, Kraus, Stinespring and Choi forms, the Pauli transfer matrix, and the channels every QRC paper uses (reset, amplitude damping, dephasing, depolarising).

Lindblad Dynamics (#/qrc/open-systems/lindblad-dynamics): the GKSL equation, T1 and T2, the Liouvillian as a matrix, its spectrum, gap and steady state, and how dissipation sets a reservoir's memory time.

Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points): trace distance and its operational meaning, contraction coefficients, fixed points of channels, conserved quantities that break the echo state property, and the conditions under which an input-driven quantum system has fading memory.

Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement): POVMs, back-action, shot noise and sample complexity, which observables can share shots, and weak measurement as a trade between information and disturbance.

blocks.text: How this connects to the rest of the shelf

items: The Fujii–Nakajima spin reservoir on The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) is exactly 'reset one qubit (a channel), then evolve unitarily': its memory comes entirely from the reset.

Whether that is enough to forget depends on the Hamiltonian; Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) shows that conserved quantities (integrable or localised regimes) spoil it, which is the fixed-point story of this topic.
Added dissipation (Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource)) and natural hardware noise turn the T1/T2 physics of the Lindblad page into a tuning knob.
Measurement back-action and shot noise (Resource Accounting (#/qrc/hardware/resource-accounting)) set the real cost of running any of this.
